utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are to continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mesic, during his testimony, was asked, that is on page 10572 of the transcript, to ask the -- he was asked to explain the financing of the JNA. He was asked by the other side to ask what he knows about financing the JNA, what budget it came from, and who had control over this budget. First and foremost, how the JNA was financed. He explained, inter alia: "[In English] This was from the revenue of the federation. The original revenue of the federation. Croatia and other republics were against this because they wanted to keep the original revenue within the republics." [Interpretation] Do you know about that? Do you know what happened at the time concerning financing the JNA from the federal budget, and on the basis of what this kind of position was taken in particular republics and why? What was the motive for taking such a stand?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was always financed from the federal budget. All republics paid a certain quota, as is done in any budget. This quota depended on the population of a respective republic and the degree of economic development. Slovenia and Croatia, on the very eve of the war, tried not to contribute to the federal budget at all, therefore to the JNA as well. However, that was unconstitutional and unlawful behaviour. The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, according to the constitution in 1974, had very few powers of its own, but foreign policy and defence were its sole and basic powers. Also, customs duties and a few other things, but those were the two basic ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, he says -- the question is actually: "[In English] Had there been a time when Croatia's contributions to the republican budget for the purposes of the JNA ceased?"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it stopped sometime after Tudjman came to power but I cannot tell you exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the explanation that he gives: "Croatia made this decision at a point in time when the army was [In English] in the service of the aggressors, when it was working on creating a Greater Serbia [Realtime transcript read in error "Great Britain"], and so Croatia could no longer continue paying this army to its own detriment." [Interpretation] Now, my question to you, Mr. Seselj, is the following: This pertains to 1991. That is the next page, 10573.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. There's a mistake in the transcript. Instead of "Greater Serbia," we have "Great Britain."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "Greater Serbia" in the transcript I'm reading from. Oh, this transcript from here. It is equally convincing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I guess it's been corrected. It says here on this page 10573: "[In English] By the time that we are dealing with, the middle of 1991 or late in 1991, were Croatian representatives still on the board of governor --" [Interpretation] on the board of governors of the National Bank? So he explains that mid-1991 was the time when financing the army stopped because the army was working on the creation of a Greater Serbia. Can you remember who was federal Prime Minister throughout 1991 and who held all the main federal posts in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal Prime Minister in all of 1991 was a Croat, Ante Markovic, and his government was in place sometime until June 1992. However, as far as I can remember, the Croatian contributions to the federal budget stopped already in 1990 because the regime of Franjo Tudjman started using that money for illegally arming Croatian paramilitary formations. The first idea that Franjo Tudjman had was that the Territorial Defence of Croatia should be turned into the army of a separate Republic of Croatia. However, the Yugoslav People's Army reached a timely decision to take over all the arms depots of the Territorial Defence in all republics and in this way Tudjman's intention was thwarted. Then Tudjman established the so-called National Guards Corps, the ZNG as it was called, and he started buying or receiving gifts of large quantities of weapons from foreign countries. Most of the weapons arrived in convoys via Hungary. Most were from the depots of the former --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you, you answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in that year 1990 or 1991, or generally speaking, when Mesic was the presiding member of the collective Commander-in-Chief and then Ante Markovic from Croatia as well was the federal Prime Minister, were there any signs of the JNA doing anything against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such thing. However, those two Croats in the top state leadership, Ante Markovic and Stipe Mesic, insisted the most on the Yugoslav People's Army intervening in Slovenia, and a decision was reached by the federal government that the army should take over the border posts in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Slovenia, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and JNA units went there without any ammunition. That is when JNA soldiers were massacred in Slovenia, and then there was a real military intervention that did not take very long. Stipe Mesic and Ante Markovic wanted to fully compromise the JNA. As far as Slovenia is concerned, no one in the remaining part of Yugoslavia had any reason to prevent Slovenia from seceding, because there were no ethnic squabbles there. Slovenia, as a federal republic, took up the territory exactly where the Slovenian people lived. It is only Slovenia itself that could have had territorial aspirations towards Croatia because part of the Slovenian people lived in Croatia and they were systematically being turned into Croats. As for Slovenian separatism, had there been a goodwill, it was possible to reach agreement at federal level. However, Stipe Mesic and Ante Markovic did not allow that. It was in their interest to have an armed conflict in Slovenia, for the army to be compromised there, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any case when the JNA - now let's leave Slovenia aside - that the JNA anywhere at the time in -- even in Croatia, intervened at any place where it was not attacked or where it went out to separate the parties that were in conflict?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the answer. No, you're not aware. Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I shall try to avoid these long quotations from the transcript. That seems to be too long. So I shall try to summarise the statements of various witnesses in these transcripts. Stipe Mesic, on the 2nd of October, 2002, that is page 10639 in the transcript, he said, when referring to you personally, that the Serb minister who was in government was one of the ministers of Mr. Milosevic, that he visited the Karlovac-Karlobag-Virovitica border together with the Chetnik vojvoda Vojislav Seselj in order to show how far the interests of Serbia went. Is that correct, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Milosevic, if you look at the transcript, particularly Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to observe a pause between question and answer. It particularly applies to Mr. Seselj who doesn't wait at all. This is not a conversation in the living-room between Mr. Milosevic and yourself. We have interpreters, and they have the job of interpreting what you say. So be a little patient, observe the pause, so that we can have the best results from them. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this morning I've really been trying to speak as slowly as possible, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not just speaking slowly. It's observing the pause after Mr. Milosevic's question so that the interpreter will have a chance of interpreting what he says before you speak. But we also want you to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, a border was never established on the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. This is part of the ideological programme of the Serb Radical Party. Secondly, I never toured that particular line with any minister or did I tour any front line with any minister from Serbia or Yugoslavia. And thirdly, never in my life was I in Ogulin. Never in my life was I in Karlovac. Never in my life was I in Virovitica. And once in my life I passed through Karlobag when I travelled from Zadar via Gospic to Bosnia. Once in my life, sometime in 1975, if my memory serves me well. So this is totally an invention on Mesic's part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for financing the army, Mesic explained that when they stopped financing the army, that the army took credits from the National Bank of Yugoslavia and the National Bank of Yugoslavia was under my control. Do you know how the National Bank of Yugoslavia functioned and who made up the board of governors of the National Bank of Yugoslavia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The board of governors of the National Bank of Yugoslavia consisted of representatives of all federal states. It was absolutely impossible for you to exercise control over the National Bank of Yugoslavia. The National Bank of Yugoslavia was to a large part under the control of the government of Ante Markovic. Ante Markovic, at the beginning of 1990, even carried out a monetary reform, and then he made it possible to sell foreign exchange freely from the reserves of the country. Since Slovenia and Croatia had the largest quantities of this money that was on bank accounts - not banknotes but simply money that was on bank accounts, electronic money as we might call it nowadays - most foreign exchange was bought by Slovenians and Croats from the federal foreign exchange reserves, which were $10 billion. So the coffers were depleted very quickly. Slovenia and Croatia were getting ready to secede, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and they were in a hurry to get as much foreign currency as possible from the federal reserves. This caused an even deeper economic crisis in Serbia, Bosnia, Montenegro, and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of October, 2002, that is page 10674, he said that in Serbia there were 18 camps where Croat citizens were held and that they were fleeing from Seselj.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a total fabrication. There was not a single camp in Serbia where Croat citizens were put up. At the beginning of the war, it was only the JNA that had Croatian prisoners of war, members of paramilitary units who were taken prisoner after fighting. For a while they would put them up at the correctional facility in Sremska Mitrovica. That is one of the prisons in Serbia that is one of the better equipped prisons, with better facilities and so on. It is far more comfortable, say, than the prison in Pozarevac. As far as I know, prisoners of war were never taken to Pozarevac. However, this went on for a very short period of time. I think that all these prisoners of war were released very soon and unilaterally at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the JNA used part of the prison facilities for that purpose, were these facilities under the control of the Ministry of Justice of Serbia or under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, JNA control. Part of the prison was separated and put under the control of the JNA command in charge. Prisoners of war, according to our regulations, could not be sent to civilian prisons. They were not detainees, they were prisoners of war. The difference in status is a major one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again, on the 3rd of October, that is to say the following day, in his testimony on page 10782, he says one minister came to the Karlovac-Karlobag-Virovitica line in the company of Vojislav Seselj whose units were also in the area. There are a few questions there, but there is one basic question: Did you have any military units at all; and if so, as Mesic says, were you in the area?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any military units. I never toured the area, as Mesic claims. And all volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were within the JNA. They were in Western Slavonia, and they were at part of the western front, in Lika approximately. They were transported there by military aircraft to the Udbina air field and then were deployed from there. It was the JNA commands in charge that deployed them. It is not serious to testify in that way. Mr. Mesic is the president of a republic. He could have at least made an effort to try to find out from the services that he is in charge of to find out what name of that -- what the name of that minister is. He is not serious for a head of state to say a Serbian minister. Whenever I speak here I make an effort to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we are now going to deal with some other witnesses that were called here. Nikola Samardzic testified here. Do you remember who Nikola Samardzic was?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, he was a minister in the government of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He stated that my policy was the creation of a Greater Serbia, and he spoke about the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line, and he said that you were my candidate for the president of this kind of Serbia. Do you have any comment on this? We're talking about his testimony of the 10th of October, 2002. As for the page of the transcript containing this testimony of his, it is page 11427, 11428, and 11429.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard anything so stupid in all my life that I was your candidate for any office let alone the top office in the land. I didn't even want ministers from my party to join a coalition government with you in 1993 let alone that you would be counting on giving me even higher office. Secondly, you absolutely had nothing to do with the concept of a Greater Serbia. The concept of a Greater Serbia and the western Serbian boundary along the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line is purely an ideological project of the Serb Radical Party. No other political party ever stood behind that project, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any translation. I didn't hear the translation of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask Mr. Milosevic, then, to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Milan Babic testified here as a witness, and he stated that Martic was my man and Goran Hadzic was his yes man. Do you know anything about that from the time when you met both Martic and Hadzic? We didn't mention them, apart from going through that list of participants in the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely untrue. The truth is that the public sentiment in Serbia was always in favour of Milan Martic, because the public thought of him as the better and the more honest man. He was not a great statesman, but he was known to live very modestly, that he was never bent on any sort of crime, that he is a very honourable and courageous person, and that explains the popularity he had among the Serbian people, the entire Serbian people. As a statesman, Milan Babic was much more capable than Milan Martic. However, his public image was always tainted by hints of low morality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On pages 13671 to 679, Milan Babic stated that I bought weapons.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, too, is nonsense. In 1991, there was a press conference where I released a propaganda balloon, so to speak, saying that volunteers of the Serb Radical Party purchased weapons through Hungary. It was an allusion to the fact that Croats were buying weapons from Hungary, and I was -- this was a tit-for-tat sort of thing. That caused a great public outcry and indignation, and I remember that even investigation was started to see if one of the ministers was involved. The truth was very different. The truth was that most of our weapons came from the depots of the Territorial Defence. They were obsolete Thompsons, and later they were weapons of JNA issue. That's what you do in politics. You say something for propaganda purposes, and that causes an effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic says on page 13803 of the transcript, and I want to ask you if it's correct, that the JNA was protecting only the Serbs while assaulting all other ethnic communities. Is that true what he says, that the JNA protected only Serbs and attacked everybody else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For several months the JNA was completely passive, without responding at all to the attacks of Croats on JNA barracks, depots, and even JNA personnel and families of personnel on the territory of Croatia. JNA was engaged in preventing armed conflict between Territorial Defence members and Croatian paramilitary units. It stood between the warring parties and tried to put an end to hostilities. It was only in August 1991 that JNA got involved into a real armed clash when the attacks on its units became massive and frequent and caused great casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic stated here on the 19th of November, 2002, page 13051 and 052, that I gave you orders as to what your party should do because I thought of you as one of the greatest patriots at that time, and that continued all the way to our personal conflict in 1993.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to think that you did think of me as a patriot always, even at the time when we clashed personally, but it is silly to say that you gave me orders at any stage of our relationship, whether it was good or it was strained by tension and conflict. All of Serbia knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the entire Serbia also knows the kind of farce we are participating in with this indictment of Mr. Nice's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a remark --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Seselj has to stop answering while Mr. Milosevic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, the comment that you made is entirely inappropriate. And, Mr. Seselj, you must observe the pause. The interpreters have just made another request. In fact, you start responding even before Mr. Milosevic has finished his question. That is -- that is normal in ordinary conversation in a living-room, but here we have technical matters to attend to and you must observe the pause, otherwise it's exceedingly difficult for the interpreters. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 2002 - and that's on transcript page 13052 to 13054 - Milan Babic described your visit of the 2nd May, 1991. That's the occasion when he said -- when you were said to use a JNA helicopter organised by Minister Marko Negovanovic, and you were said to ask for that helicopter calling from the office of Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's untrue, beginning with the date. On the 2nd of May, I was leading the peace march to Plitvice, although Milan Babic was initially the leader. But when he saw the soldiers with their rifles cocked, he got frightened and retreated to the back of the column. I travelled by helicopter from Knin in November 1991. About the office of Milan Babic, it's true that I called Marko Negovanovic from that office, but I called him as chief of General Staff, whereupon Marko Negovanovic told me to call General Vukovic, who I think was commander of the Knin Corps at the time. General Vukovic invited me to his staff, to his headquarters. I went there. From his headquarters I also talked to Colonel Mladic, and then General Vukovic provided me with a helicopter to go to Mostar. He announced my arrival, and in Mostar another helicopter waited for me. Those were small helicopters, Gazelle type. It was impossible for me to go directly from Knin to Belgrade or from Knin to Podgorica, so I went from Knin to Mostar, from Mostar to Podgorica, and from Podgorica I took a commercial line to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think you gave us an exhaustive answer. Just tell me, because I didn't remember correctly, did you say that Marko Negovanovic was chief of General Staff or assistant chief?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was actually deputy chief of General Staff. At any rate, he wasn't the minister of defence of Serbia. The defence minister at the time was Mr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had another witness here, Jovan Dunic [as interpreted]. He testified to an event in Vukovar. Do you know the name of Jovan Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I have been in contact with Jovan Dulovic once, but it was after the war. He was a correspondence of Ekspres Politika newspaper from Vukovar for the duration of the liberation struggle for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Vukovar, and he wrote reports full of praise for the fighters of the JNA and the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. And then sometimes -- sometime in 1995, he became a journalist of the spying agency that is the Vreme magazine in Belgrade. It has been published since end 1990, with a very small circulation, 5 to 6.000 copies, but it is continuously financed by Western intelligence services and various other Western agencies and branches. When he joined the Vreme magazine, he changed his ideological perceptions completely and started taking part in the anti-Serb propaganda political campaign. I provided the Office of the Prosecutor, in the course of proceedings against me, two documents to announce my special Defence, as stipulated by the Rules of Evidence and Procedure. In those two documents I provided a wealth of intelligence data that I got hold of through my men in the state security service. This intelligence is highly confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm stopping you because I believe you have answered the question. It's for Mr. Milosevic to put another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this intelligence that you provided, what does it have to do with? What is it related to, and what does it have to do with Jovan Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this intelligence one can see that Jovan Dulovic was engaged in subversive and spying activities for the benefit of various Western intelligence agencies. I provided these documents to the Office of the Prosecutor and published them also in my book called The Devil's Apprentice, The Criminal Roman Pope John Paul II. The Prosecutor who is in charge of my case can tell you this. It has been translated into English and the Prosecution can easily get hold of these documents. These documents completely disqualify and discredit both Jovan Dulovic and Mr. Anastasijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us deal with some of these assertions. I have a note here regarding the testimony of Anastasijevic as well. Tell me about this salto mortale by Jovan Dulovic. It happened in 1995.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when he got on the payroll of Western intelligence agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He testified here and he mentioned the date of the 12th of November, 1991. He was testifying about Vukovar. So on the 12th of November, 1991, according to his testimony, there was a meeting between you and Mr. Radic, a JNA officer; Mr. Bojkovski; and Stanko Vujanovic. Those are the people he mentioned. And some other officers were involved, plus this witness Jovan Dulovic, who says that he attended personally that meeting where you stated, "All of us are one army." I don't see what's so special about saying this, "All of us are one army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, put the question and stop the comments. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 12th of November, 1995 -- 1991, correction, there was this meeting allegedly with a group of officers. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Dulovic is making all that up. There was no such meeting, quite simply. I toured the entire town of Vukovar up to the front lines. I went everywhere, and I met with all sorts of people. But the only real formal meeting I had with officers took place when the then Colonel, currently General, Mrksic organised a dinner for me in his commander tent. There was his ADC Colonel Panic, another group of officers, there could have been Sljivancanin, there could have been Radic, and there was no other meeting at all. However, I have a different piece of information. In the case against me as part of the public documents, Dulovic asserts that he did not attend the meeting. He says he was standing on the stairs, that the door was open, and that's how he overheard the conversation. As for the statement itself or, rather, the testimony itself, I absolutely do not trust people who claim they can remember such things 15 years later. But it's true that everywhere where I went to tour the front line -- Mr. Robinson, this is very important because I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped you. Let Mr. Milosevic elicit it from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have just explained that he overheard that standing on the stairs, and you say that this meeting was held in a tent.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I claim that Jovan Dulovic did not attend that dinner. And as for my position, my general position, I have always been against paramilitary units everywhere and anywhere, and I always insisted that all fighting men be within the JNA, and that could be an explanation for my statement, "All of us are one army." "We are all one army." That's what I said in the media and everywhere. I was in favour of the preservation of the JNA and against any paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since it was unclear here what in fact he said, I have to quote from the transcript, practically at the insistence of Mr. Robinson, because it's not clear what he said. He mentioned the date of the 12th of November. I'll skip most of his testimony, and I'll start with the passage where he mentions you. That's on page 11683. "[In English] Did there come a time when the person you've described as Vojislav Seselj arrived at that house?" "Yes." [Interpretation] I'll skip. It was 6.00, 6.30 p.m. "[In English] He came with his entourage. They were armed." [Interpretation] So he talks about the fact that you had arrived at some house where the officers I mentioned were already gathered. Radic and others. Sljivancanin seems to have come by. Sasa Bojkovski and many other officers. "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... detachment attending meeting." [Interpretation] So all those people were there when you came with armed people accompanying you. Is any of that description correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely impossible that such a meeting took place. I don't exclude the possibility that I entered a house. I entered many houses of the Serbs living there. People invited me in. I wanted to see how people were living under wartime conditions. During my stay, for example, a mine exploded and killed a soldier who was riding either a bicycle or a motorcycle, and he resided nearby. He was a local man from Vukovar. So I went to visit his family to express my condolences. There were many encounters, but there was no meeting apart from this dinner in the command tent of the then Colonel, now General, Mrksic. I assert that decidedly. Secondly, I was armed. I had an automatic rifle. I wore a uniform. I was always accompanied by several soldiers, by several volunteers. I had only one person escorting me from Belgrade, Petar Panic. He was my personal escort at the time. Nobody else had arrived with me from Belgrade. But I was always surrounded by soldiers, and I visited all the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the people you were with were not your escort, they were simply people you were having conversations with.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only one person escorting me who came from Belgrade, Petar Panic. There may have been a driver as well. I can't recall precisely now. But I usually drove my own personal car wherever I went, even to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was asked by the other side: "[In English] Can you describe what happened when Mr. Seselj entered the building?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Together with the officers, with Radic and Bojkovski and Stanko Jovanovic as well as some other officers from artillery units, he went into the largest room in that house where a meeting was held." "Where were you when this meeting was being held?" [Interpretation] Answer: "[In English] The table was right next to the door, and I was at a table right next to the door of that room. The door was slightly ajar, and one could hear what was being said inside. "Were you able to hear Mr. Seselj when he spoke during the meeting? "Very clearly. "And were you able to identify -- the voice that you heard clearly, were you able to identify it as the voice of Mr. Seselj? "Absolutely." [Interpretation] Then he goes on to explain in answer to the question of whether he heard what you said and whether he noted down your words, he says: "[In English] Yes. "How did you record his words? [Interpretation] He explains that he still has your words in his notebook, as it says here, and that he can repeat them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for a question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a very lengthy explanation. He's explaining where his notebook is but he didn't bring it to Court, and he quotes what you said. And that's on page 11687. "[In English] 'We are all one army. This war is a great test for Serbs. Those who pass the test will become winners. Deserters cannot go unpunished. Not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive.'" [Interpretation] Did you say this, Mr. Seselj, what Dulovic says here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dulovic, while reporting from Vukovar, wrote that I insisted that soldiers, primarily volunteers, be extremely disciplined, that I was against drunkenness, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the question was did you say what Dulovic has attributed to you, which is: "This war is a great test for Serbs. Deserters cannot go unpunished, and not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement itself makes no sense because there was no meeting. Much of what Dulovic said corresponds to my positions and my public statements, but he couldn't have quoted my precise words. You're putting a question to me based on a fabrication whether I said this at a meeting which I say never took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, you have the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't have the answer, I don't think. I thought you indicated that there was a meeting and that he was listening to this meeting from a position he should not have been in. Are we now talking about a different event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said there was a dinner in the command staff of Colonel Mrksic. Dulovic was not present, and Dulovic is not testifying about that dinner. He claims there was another meeting apart from this meeting where I made a statement like this, in somebody's house. And this is a fabrication. There was no other meeting. There was only the meeting in the tent of Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it possible that these things were said at the dinner you're referring to? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hold political speeches at that dinner. It wouldn't have made any sense. At that dinner we discussed how the operations were progressing, what the problems were, what was going on on the ground. These were all high-ranking officers. Why should I make speeches to them saying we're all one army and so on and so forth? We had serious matters to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you the question again: Is it possible you said that at the meeting or at the dinner? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at that dinner. These are very general things. I could have said that elsewhere but not at that dinner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, did you ever say those words at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That we're all one army, that was my general political standpoint. It was also my standpoint that the Ustasha had to be defeated, that not a single Ustasha could leave alive but that they should all be caught. And if they were caught alive, they should be tried. I advocated in public that they be tried. I made statements on Serbian radio in Vukovar, calling on Croatian policemen and paramilitary men to surrender, saying that they would be guaranteed the kind of treatment that is provided for in the regulations and the treatment of prisoners of war. Those are things I said in public and on Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You have explained the motives and the background. You have also provided a document where one can establish how credible this witness is and how reliable. Let's move on, Mr. Seselj. Borislav Jovic said here that the Serb Yugoslav leadership never wanted a Greater Serbia and that there were three options, and those were, first to preserve Yugoslavia through constitutional changes; second, should Yugoslavia dissolve, organise a referendum at which nations would be given the right to self-determination; and thirdly, ensuring equality for Serbs in republics outside Yugoslavia. He testified on the 19th of November, 2003, and this is on pages 29215 to 29216 of the transcript. He mentioned those three options. I hope you remember what I quoted to you. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically it's correct, because in Yugoslav constitutional legal theory and practice, there was never any mention of the right of federal units to self-determination, including secession. There was only the right of nations to self-determination. But this did not include secession, because this was considered to be a one-time right and that all the nations in the former Yugoslavia had used that right after World War II when they opted to live in Yugoslavia as a federal state of equal republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. Seselj, how that fits with the views you've expressed this morning about Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you my views. On the other hand, in a situation where the country was facing dissolution, the question arose as to whether Slovenia should be kept within Yugoslavia by force, and yet there were no unsolved ethnic issues there. To start with, the position of the majority political factors was that Slovenia should not be allowed to secede either. I was the first to advocate granting that right to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But is the short answer that you would say that you accepted the basis for Slovenia seceding, but strictly speaking, their secession did not fit with the legal regime? They ought to have followed a different course, but because of the make-up of the population, you accepted that what they did was not unreasonable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was unlawful, there is no doubt about it. But to avoid war, in my view it was better to let Slovenia go peacefully than clash with the Slovenian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with what Jovic said here.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was true. Was it also true what Jovic said here? It's on page 29272 of the transcript, that the political leadership, our political leadership was afraid there would be a genocide of Serbs in Croatia, as had happened previously in history.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what all Serbs were afraid of. This was a pervasive fear throughout the entire Serb people, because Tudjman openly expressed his will to have continuity with the former Independent State of Croatia, which was Hitler's satellite state. He revived this ideology. He said that this fascist creation had been the expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people, and after that, everything was clear to the Serbs; the Serbs could expect nothing good from Tudjman's state. There was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have been through this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic said here, and this is on page 29380 and 381, that in Cleveland in February 1990, Tudjman said that the main goal of his party was to separate Croatia from Yugoslavia. In February 1990, Tudjman was not in power yet. Do you recall this statement made by Tudjman in Cleveland?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Tudjman's tour in America and Canada, all of it, and this was not the only such statement he made. Wherever he spoke, this was the position he advocated. It was part of his election campaign and his platform. On the basis of this, he collected vast sums of money from the Croatian Ustasha emigres community. He also made such statements in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To complete Mr. Jovic's testimony, he said, and that's page 29273 and 4, it's a political standpoint that was pervasive at the time, that Croatia and Slovenia had been recognised too soon by Germany and this speeded up the crisis and led to war. Is this your understanding of the events at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Borisav Jovic overlooked a fact here. It was the Vatican that first recognised the independence of Croatia, followed by Germany. But it did speed up the course of events leading to war and the dissolution of Yugoslavia. This recognition took place after the adoption of the Vance Plan, when a peaceful solution had to be sought. Something similar happened in Bosnia. The Cutileiro Plan was adopted, and right after that independence was recognised and war broke out. So those who, after the adoption of peace plans, unilaterally recognised independence in an unlawful manner because it could not be recognised if the central government did not have control over the entire territory under international law, so that independence could only have been recognised on the territory not including the Krajina. Therefore, those who did this unilaterally, first the Vatican, then Germany, then the European Community and then America, they caused new wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 292738 and 9, Jovic said that I opposed the establishment of a Serb army. Can you challenge this or confirm it? And also answer the question of who in Serbia was in favour of establishing a Serb army.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those in authority in Serbia were opposed to the establishing of a Serb army. They all fought for the preservation of Yugoslavia and the JNA, including you personally and your party. However, the situation was different among the opposition parties. In the opposition, it was only the Serb Radical Party that was in favour of preserving the JNA, but we also advocated the reform of the JNA, primarily the removal of communist symbols. The pro-Western political parties wanted to abolish the JNA and form a Serb army because they wanted Serb separatism, and on the other hand they wanted to create a basis for Serbia and the government in Serbia if a Serb army set up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago when talking about Dulovic, you mentioned Dejan Anastasijevic, another witness here. He testified here first as K1 and later on under his own name. He said that he interviewed you several times. He said that you were my nationalist satellite and that on one occasion you said to him that in the period from 1991 to 1992 you had very close friendly relations with Jovica Stanisic and that your cooperation with him pertained to the organisation of paramilitary formations in Croatia and Bosnia. You can find that on 11480 and 481, those pages of the transcript, the evidence given by Dejan Anastasijevic. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dejan Anastasijevic first of all was a spy of the State Security Service of Serbia. Then Western intelligence agencies took him over. And that is not the only such example. That was the case of Goran Svilanovic and some others. Secondly, I've already said that I first met Jovica Stanisic in November 1992. However, in 1993, when there was a fierce clash between the Serb Radical Party, the Socialist Party of Serbia -- and the Socialist Party of Serbia, I launched an all-out propaganda offensive against you personally and against the Socialist Party of Serbia and Jovica Stanisic as head of state security. I have to say here quite openly that in this propaganda offensive I did not choose my methods to tarnish your name, insult you in public, to do anything that would cause hatred and rage on your part. I had a direct reason for doing that. Your party first attacked me in a press release, that I was a criminal, that I was a madman, that I was an alcoholic. I, who perhaps just have a sip of alcohol a few times a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you wanted to say in connection with what he said here, that you had an excellent relationship in terms of engaging paramilitaries in Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic, as head of the state security, after the head-on clash between our two parties, started arresting volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, and he started issuing press releases to the effect that they were arrested as criminals, and they would find one or two pieces of weapons on each and every one of them. The state television showed footage of some arms depots found God knows where. All these volunteers who were arrested were accused of being war criminals. That is what was said to the public. What happened was that a month later they would be released. None of them were ever prosecuted. I think that some of them were punished for misdemeanors, though. The state security service in this way arrested volunteers for no reason whatsoever, and that is why I pulled all stops as far as Jovica Stanisic was concerned. Whatever first came to mind is what I said about Jovica Stanisic in public. He was the most powerful man in the secret service. He was considered to be the most powerful person in Serbia. Many people said that he was the most powerful person after you. And I really pulled all stops. I did not choose my methods of attacking him. Now, perhaps this Hague Prosecution wrote indictments against you and Jovica Stanisic on the basis of press articles or my own statements. However, that will make it easier to challenge their indictments. So -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What Dejan Anastasijevic says, namely that he interviewed you several times, is that correct? Why do you think he is not a reliable witness?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we had only one conversation. You know, I cannot remember exactly what he looked like when I talked to him because I talked to a multitude of journalists. At any rate, he did interview me. That interview was published in the Vreme magazine and it's easy to find, so that's very easy to clarify. As for Dejan Anastasijevic, I found his entire file at the state security service. I have a rarefied network. I have people everywhere. I even have people in The Hague Office of the Prosecutor, and I received valuable documents from there, too. For example, I published what Jovica Stanisic said to The Hague Office of the Prosecutor. I'm a man who knows what he's doing. I look for what I need, and I find what I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions he spoke about you. On the 27th of September, 2002 - that is 10341 and 342 - when asked about a map of Yugoslavia where some lines were drawn, the witness explained that this line is based on a line that Seselj talked about. In Seselj's perception, those are the new borders of the Serb state, a Greater Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot exactly discern what the witness said quite specifically, but it is true indeed that the Serb Radical Party made a map, a geographical map of a Greater Serbia with western ethnic borders on the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. And the Serb Radical Party has the exclusive right of authorship over that line. It was only the Serb Radical Party that ever advocated that. No one else, either in Serbia or Republika Srpska or the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was half of the question. I'm going to quote page 10343, 4 and 5 now. It says: "Seselj had in mind a state that would include Serbs only. As for Croats, the best thing would be for them to go to Croatia. Albanians should live in Albania." The witness cannot recall whether Seselj spoke about Bosniaks. And -- or, rather, let's deal with this first. At that time, you had in mind a state that would include Serbs only, and for the Croats it would be best to go to Croatia and Albanians to live in Albania.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policy of the Serb Radical Party and of me personally was that this Serb state should include practically all Serbs, Serbs who were Orthodox, Serb Catholics, Serbs who were Muslims, and so on. I advocated the expulsion of Albanian emigres who did not acquire our citizenship and who were active from separatist positions. I could not have referred to any kind of Bosniaks because the Bosniak nation was invented much later, in 1994 and 1995, whenever. So this is the latest invention as far as these nations are concerned. The Serb Radical Party always consistently advocated the full equality of rights of the members of all national minorities in our territory, and that is why our membership included Hungarians, Romanians, Bulgarians, and members of all other national minorities; Slovaks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you talk of Serb Catholics in this context are you referring to people who would normally regard themselves as domiciled in Serbia or are you talking about the Serb Catholics you described earlier who nowadays regard themselves as Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Serb Catholics who consider themselves to be Croats today. In 1900, the Catholic Congress was held in Zagreb where it was first proclaimed that all Catholics who spoke the Serbo-Croat or Croato-Serb language, as it was called at the time, were Croats. Now, what was it that happened? First the Croats espoused the Serb language as their own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't require you to go into that detail. Does it follow from that answer that when you talk about Serbs who were Muslims you're talking about people who would normally regard themselves as Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As of a few years ago they've been calling themselves Bosniaks, yes. I am talking about them. Because all top intellectuals from the ranks of the so-called Croats and the so-called Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, I don't need an explanation of the history. I'm quite happy with an indication of your view and who you're referring to when you talk about these folk. I was simply looking for clarification, and you've provided that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order for this to be complete, Mr. Seselj, let us digress slightly. Do you know about the Yugoslav author Mesa Selimovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mehmet Mesa Selimovic is a Muslim from Bosnia and one of the greatest Serb authors of all time. He said for himself, "I am a Serb, my family is Serb, my father was a Serb, we're all Serbs." In his last will and testament he said that because he knew that after his death somebody would try to claim him, saying that he belonged to an invented nation. Mehmed Mesa Selimovic, Hasan Kikic, Skender Kulenovic, Camil Sijaric, and so on and so forth. All these top intellectuals who were Muslims emphasised that they were Serbs. And also among these alleged Croats, Ivan Gundulic and all the writers from Dubrovnik. Then Ivo Vojnovic, Ivan Stojanovic, Milan Resetar, Vladimir Dvornikovic, all the way up to Ivo Andric. All of them are Catholics, but they were proud of the fact that they belonged to the Serb nation. Artificially, later on, Serb Catholics were turned into Croats. First they were forced to declare themselves as Croats, and after brainwashing they said that they were Croats en masse. And after several decades of brainwashing, now the Muslims are convinced that they are some kind of a nation in its own right, and now even that has been changed and they're called Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mesa Selimovic, and we know that he is one of the most prominent Serb writers, in his last will and testament, which he left in the Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts, he wrote that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That text was published in his book called Secanja, "Memories."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that will do as for this particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have to remind you of Josif Pancic. Josif Pancic is a Serb who is a Catholic and he was the first Serb -- the first person who was president of the Royal Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts, and there are many other examples to that effect. In my book The Ideology of Serb Nationalism, there is a special chapter devoted to Serb Catholics, giving a series of examples. Yet another chapter about Serb Muslims with specific examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: C037, a witness here, said in addition to what you've been saying just now, that at that time Seselj was very prominent in the press, radio and television. All his speeches were reported about. Journalists followed him everywhere. This includes state television. He was given total freedom of speech. Could you please explain this to me. What does that mean, that you were given total freedom of speech? Would that mean that somebody was not given total freedom of speech in Serbia in the 1990s? Who was it who had total freedom of speech and who was it that did not have total freedom of speech? Please give us examples for both.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible for me to answer that because after half a century of communist dictatorship, your government was the first one, Mr. Milosevic, that introduced full freedom of speech and freedom of thought. Full freedom. And it is not true that I figured most prominently in the media. After the elections in 1992, Snezana Milivojevic, together with another associate whose name I cannot remember, published a book. If I remember correctly, it was called The Elections On Screen. And in that book, on the basis of empirical data, she showed that the Serb Radical Party was the least represented party in the media when compared to other political parties. Our use of the media was the most effective because we are one of the few political parties that had a feeling of conviction deep down in terms of what we were advocating, our political views. Among all the people who were deceitful, we shone brilliantly as people who believed in their own ideology. That is what made us different. And we expressed our readiness to sacrifice ourself for our ideas, as opposed to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you arrived in The Hague on your own when you heard that there was an indictment against you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I happened to be arrested at the airport. I wanted to come to The Hague. For ten years I offered myself to The Hague. I phoned them several times, the Office of the Prosecutor here, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What Mr. Seselj said at the end is not included in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He said he offered himself to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have been sad, truly sad had I not come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a complete picture now, Mr. Seselj. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10346, the same witness, C037, says non-Serbs were not desirable in the territory of Krajina. This was first said by Seselj, and Serbs from other territories would come to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that's untrue. I never said that non-Serbs were undesirable in Krajina. I'll tell you one detail. When I was in Mirkovci during the war, there was a unit of local TO, and some Croats were in the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to stop you. You have answered the question. The tendency to go on and on and on has to be checked. You did answer the question. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same witness says he does not remember you were involved in the incident in Plitvice. And as for the meeting in Srb, you were present but it was not agreed in advance, you just dropped by. Is that true about your presence in the Krajina, and did he present it correctly?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it's true I attended the rally in Srb, but I didn't speak there. There was Jovan Raskovic, Milan Babic, and other speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He says you were not involved in the Plitvice incident.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that happened a month before my arrival, sometime in March. Croatian special police barged in that place, there was a clash, and as far as I remember one Croatian policeman was killed and one Serb policeman before a JNA unit arrived to calm down the tensions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Later on, I took part in the protest march of the Serbian people towards Plitvice, and that was on the 2nd May, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 10429, the same witness, C037, testifying on the 30th of September, 2002, says that in Balinci and in Bacin crimes were perpetrated by Seselj's radicals with the help, of course, of local extremists. That's his assertion. So the two places are Balinci and Bacin, crimes allegedly perpetrated by Seselj's radicals with the help of local extremists.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of a single crime allegedly perpetrated by volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. We were very strict. Even for minor offences, theft, robbery and such, we expelled such people from the party and suggested that they be expelled from the units as well. I never heard of a single volunteer of the Serb Radical Party perpetrating a more serious crime. There was not a singe instance of that. JNA officers and commanders always held them up as an example to emulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10431, he says that in Vocin there were volunteers from the ranks of Seselj's radicals and asked who killed the members of that family on the 15th December 1991. The witness says that, according to the locals, it was done by Seselj's radicals and extremists.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Our men were not involved in that. They were stationed about ten kilometres away, and they themselves were badly beaten in a village called Masicka Sagovina. A great number of volunteers was killed on that day, and an even larger number were taken prisoner. Although they were tortured as prisoners, all of them were later released. None of them were tried. It never happened that a volunteer from the Serbian Radical Party had been charged with a war crime until recently. What happened recently was that Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, found himself among the group of men on trial in Belgrade. But I have a document provided to me by the OTP, and it's a public document, from which you can see that Kameni was not involved in the Ovcara incident, and the participants in the execution in Ovcara called him all sorts of names the next day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can quote -- this is a rather bad term, maybe a profanity, Mr. Robinson. Can I say it? But it's in a public document. Will you allow me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the name they called him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the break anyhow. We'll come back to that after the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this same witness, C037, page 10434, speaks about Croat civilians who were killed in the beginning of October 1991, and he says that what was done in Balinci was done by Seselj's volunteers.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know where Balinci is located let alone something more specific. I don't really know where Balinci is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... know where Balinci is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's an impossible question. I don't know all the places where the JNA sent its units including volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. Balinci is a term that has been mentioned in reports only recently, and I don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Seselj. In view of the composition of your party, would you know whether your volunteers had perpetrated a crime?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely convinced that I would know if some of our volunteers were involved in some crimes. Somebody would immediately report it, the party would immediately intervene. But there was simply no such information. I told you, even for minor offences we immediately expelled people from the party; and second, we insisted that their units expel them too. I mentioned the case of this Zuca man who was found thieving in Eastern Slavonia, and he was immediately thrown out of the party. He later said that he left the Serbian Radical Party because we were cooperating with the regime. That much is true. But such people always tried to explain their actions by ideology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we're talking about the Serb Radical Party volunteers within the JNA, and you say that if they committed a crime as JNA members, you and your party would be informed of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's certain that in some way we would be informed. The competent JNA command would inform us. Other volunteers who are members of our party without being members of the JNA would inform us. We were convinced that our volunteers had to be the most disciplined to protect the honour of the party and its reputation. That's very important for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know you are so convinced. I know you are so convinced, but what kind of institutional relationship did the JNA have with the Serb Radical Party such that you would necessarily receive that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no institutional link. As citizens, both collectively and individually, we cooperated with and assisted the JNA. In one case, I personally addressed a letter to Colonel Trbojevic in Western Slavonia, asking that people from the Radical Party who were engaged in rallying volunteers be placed on the payroll of the JNA because their engagement in Western Slavonia lasted for months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying, then, that the only way you'd receive this kind of information would have been through informal channels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Through informal channels. But I believe that even though informal, those channels were very reliable, because our members were very conscientious in party terms, and they had great party discipline. And I'm certain that even if somebody from outside had gotten hold of such information, they would inform us immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this witness says that Seselj's radicals, that's on page 10438, robbed and murdered Stojan Bojanic in Glavica while withdrawing. He doesn't know whether it happened on the 21st or the 22nd December. This man seems to be a Serb, judging by his name. Do you about this case?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of it but it seems implausible to me that perpetrators are unknown. It is my deep conviction that every crime has a first and last name. Behind every crime there is an individual or a group and every crime can be elucidated from that aspect. The person who said Seselj's men, could easily have said the Japanese, or Martians, or anything else. I read in one submission by the Prosecution the term Seselj's White Eagles. There was also a lot of confusion. Even the OTP is unable to find its way through this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you clarified enough that White Eagles had never had anything to do with the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever. On the contrary, we always criticised other volunteer groups if they were involved in crimes. You probably remember our sharp critique of Arkan's men, Mauzer's men, and some others, the Serbian Guard, for instance. Whenever we would find out by crimes perpetrators -- perpetrated by others, we stigmatised it in public because we thought it was highly harmful to the Serb people as a whole because it was contrary to the customs and traditions of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness says on page 10441, in Sekulinci, Zvecevo, and Ceralije, Seselj's men were quartered in the area of Zvecevo facing Slatina, not other places. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party were quartered in various places in Western Slavonia, and at any given moment there were at least 500 volunteers from the SRS there. Their superior was Colonel Trbojevic and he praised them when I toured that area. I slept up there at Zvecevo. There is some sort of mountaineers lodge. That's where I spent the night. I toured various lines, and Colonel Trbojevic never ceased to praise the discipline of the volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party. He said they were among the most disciplined. That -- their stints were a month long. Sometimes 45 days. Those were people who had jobs waiting for them, families waiting for them. So they went and served on these lines in these areas for a month, month and a half, and then they would go back home and be replaced by another shift. But I believe that at every given moment there were at least 500 volunteers from the SRS distributed among various units. There were never more than one company of volunteers from the SRS in any unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10467, he says: "People were afraid of Seselj's men. They were cruel. They did all sorts of things to the local population. They intimidated them, threatened them. Some of them were involved in looting. That's what people said to me. People complained to me that they had been robbed. The local population, both Serb and Croat, mistrusted them and feared them. Seselj came and toured his units in the area of Zvecevo in December 1991. He made inspections in Vocin and Slatina. I don't know about other places. He held speeches to soldiers who were his sympathisers, but I didn't hear them. I heard about it from the local population, people who were there." So you were in Zvecevo. You toured the units that included your volunteers.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I toured many other units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let us clear this up. People were afraid of Seselj's men. They were cruel. They did all sorts of things to the local population. They looted, robbed both Croats and Serbs who were afraid of them and mistrusted them. What can you say about these assertions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to say I made inspections is an overstatement. I just toured units. I didn't have any formal authority to inspect units. But there were certain problems that I tried to help with. For instance, there was a group of volunteers that had been given old JNA uniforms, so I begged the competent commands to give them newer uniforms that were nicer. They looked better, and that they -- they were in camouflage colours. During my tours, I spoke to a lot of civilians, including a large number of Croats. I never, never came across a complaint. Everybody received me well, spoke to me nicely. We discussed general political topics and their everyday life. Most of the complaints had to do with poor supply of food and necessities and such like. I never heard a single complaint against the conduct of the volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party in Western Slavonia. However, when you have testimony that is third hand, fourth hand, fifth hand, that's worthless. This witness says, "People told me." Maybe old wives at the hairdresser's shop told him. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. You've made the point. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10959, the same witness says he didn't know anything about paramilitary units of Vuk Draskovic. He only knew about Seselj's men, and that's only based on what the population told him. So what kind of paramilitary units of yours is this a reference to? Did you have a paramilitary unit anywhere?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere. That's one thing. Another thing: The volunteers from our party in the places where they were stationed came into contact with the local population. They fraternised. And if a crime had occurred, people would know who exactly did it. These and these people committed a crime. You can't say everybody committed crimes or everybody was involved. If a crime was committed, it's not difficult to know who exactly did it by name. Such cases involving volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party are not to be found anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the description of these men as "Seselj's men" a fair one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this term "Seselj's men" can encompass various groups. I've already given you an example from the judgement in the case against Radoslav Brdjanin. I read all the judgements that were available to me. This judgement refers to a paramilitary unit of local Serbs in Bosnian Krajina called Seselj's men. I never heard of them in my life before reading that judgement, before -- because we never sent people to Bosnian Krajina. So when somebody says "Seselj's men," God knows what they mean by it. Do they mean volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party coming from Serbia? Does he mean some local Serbs who called themselves by some local name or called themselves like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what context do you consider the description to be fair and accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This description would be fair with respect to volunteers of the Serb Radical Party who were sent as volunteers to the front line as part of the JNA. They might be called Seselj's men because I motivated them to volunteer, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Nikola Samardzic on the 8th of October 2002, that's on page 11197 of the transcript, said that you led a campaign to raise the morale of soldiers around Dubrovnik, a large scale and very bad campaign. He said: "At that time he was playing his role of a Chetnik duke. He got this title from the war criminal Djuic who immigrated after World War II. This self-proclaimed Chetnik duke inspected troops wearing symbols of the Chetniks from World War I. The witness added that it was shameful that a review of a glorious, chivalrous army was carried out by someone like Seselj." So he's speaking of Dubrovnik, your review, and the insignia, as you heard, and the qualification that you were a self-proclaimed duke.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The testimony of Nikola Samardzic is absolutely untrue and contains a number -- a large number of lies. First of all, Momcilo Djuic was not a war criminal who conferred upon me the title of Chetnik duke. He lived in America, and had he been a war criminal, America would have extradited him to communist Yugoslavia as it did in the case of real criminals, such as Artukovic. He was the last one to be extradited. It never occurred to them to extradite Momcilo Djuic because he fought against the occupiers and did not commit any crimes. Secondly, I did not carry out an inspection or review. I toured the Herzegovina war front facing Dubrovnik, and I visited several front lines there. There were never any volunteers of the Serb Radical Party at the time. There were only JNA units and reservists from Montenegro. Wherever I turned up, I was welcomed. For example, when I came to Ljubinje, several hundred soldiers gathered round me and started singing "From Niksic to Split Duke Seselj is the one whose opinion is asked about." I did not carry out any inspection but I was popular among the Serb fighters and my arrival probably did help to raise morale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Just remind me, when was the title of duke conferred upon you? You told us earlier in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 28th of June, 1989, at the Serb Assembly near the Libertyville monastery near Chicago in America. Duke Momcilo Djuic had declared me the new Chetnik duke in 1989 in my absence. That was two years before the war began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in his statement of reasons, if you're interested, he said that I was a prominent anti-communist fighter in the homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Witness Jovan Dulovic says on page 11736 of the transcript Cele - that is a certain person called Miroslav Vukovic - entered Marko Pavlovic's office -- Marko Popovic, that is, or Marko Popovic, there were three or four names used to describe that man -- and put a pistol to his head. Cele was Seselj's man. This was one of Seselj's units.
