Major Pavlovic said to the witness that he had called Radmilo Bogdanovic and Seselj and Seselj had told him that Cele was from his unit, that he was beyond control --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, rather, interpreter's apology, that Cele and his unit was beyond control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- and had nothing to do with them. Was that a unit of yours?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no unit of ours, either mine or of the Serb Radical Party. Miroslav Vukovic Cele was a volunteer from the Serb Radical Party in Eastern Slavonia and Zvornik. In Zvornik he was a member of the JNA. Several years later, he was expelled from the Serb Radical Party but for completely different reasons. I never heard that Miroslav Vukovic Cele participated in any crimes. Miroslav Vukovic Cele, however, is today the president of the Association of Veterans from the wars from 1991 to 1995. He is the president of the War Veterans Association of Serbia. So he's still active in political life. Nobody ever said that he had perpetrated any crimes. And as for what Dulovic says, who knows? Maybe he did have a conflict with a Serb, but this man is neither a Croat nor a Muslim. It's possible that there was a conflict among Serbs somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And remember to observe the pause, Mr. Seselj, after Mr. Milosevic's question, because I can hear the interpreter gasping for breath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is more than one place in Jovan Dulovic's testimony where you are mentioned, and this testimony here was used to accuse me of what went on there. I will skip over some of these because they don't seem very important, and we don't have a lot of time. For example, the possibility of contacting you, the percentage of the Zvornik population that would join the Radical Party, and so on and so forth. But in answer to a question put to witness Jovan Dulovic, and that's on page 11750, did the witness personally interview Seselj when shooting a documentary film about these events, the witness answered in the affirmative. Do you recall Jovan Dulovic, on page 11753, where a video was played and the transcript says as follows: "Dulovic: Yesterday you said on television that Milosevic was the one who supplied your unit with weapons, that he took an active part in all this and that then he turned his back on you. "Seselj: Yes, that is a fact. In 1991 and 1992, Milosevic was the leading nationalist and patriot, and at that time we cooperated closely. When 30.000 paramilitary troops were sent to the front lines where the Serb people had to fight, he was the one who supplied weapons, ammunition, clothing and food, transport, military equipment, and so on." This was played here. Can you explain what you just said and what is said in this interview? Do you remember this interview?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall ever saying something like this to Jovan Dulovic, but I certainly did make such statements for various media during the vehement propaganda campaign that we started against you and your government, because you were doing the same to us. As I said, we felt that all means were permissible. We wanted to upset you as much as possible, to make you angry, to get you to take ill-considered repressive measures against the Serb Radical Party because that would have been politically favourable for us. And I have to say we did manage to get you to take such measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What measures?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that I was tried in 1994 with my collaborators and spent four months in prison, that your government and your police arrested us at Gnjilane and held us in prison for two months. So we opposed you as far as we could. And from the rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan to this showdown in 1993 where your party and secret police first moved against us, and then we waged an all-out campaign against you, and we simply did not choose our words or, rather, we chose those words we felt would upset you the most. So I cannot confirm that I said this to Jovan Dulovic, but I'm sure I said things like this to many other media. On the other hand, as you know, we were unable to speak on the state-run media, so this was a way for us to gain publicity through the opposition media. As for Jovan Dulovic, I visited Iraq in 2001. I was received by my friend Saddam Hussein, the president of Iraq. On my way back, I stopped off in Damascus and the then Yugoslav ambassador in Lebanon, the brother of Jovan Dulovic, came to see me. He came especially from Beirut to Damascus to meet me, and he started complaining to me that his brother was a traitor and a foreign mercenary. I think this is very telling and shows that Jovan Dulovic is not reliable as a witness. Jovan Dulovic could have found any number of statements of mine in other media and used them, but they cannot be used in court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There must be some limit to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the liberty the Court is going to allow this witness. I'm not going to stand up and object at all, if I can avoid it, but really we are seeing an extraordinary form of evidence given this morning and I would invite the Chamber to restrain the witness as far as it feels it should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What precisely is the point, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the last answer where we see -- if we look at the question. The question, if we can actually find it, is what measures were taken. He then elaborates upon the measures he took, or that he says he took, and then it goes on into a long explanation about his visit to Iraq and comments on the reliability of witnesses coming in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to me that Mr. Milosevic is using this witness to comment on testimony given by Prosecution witnesses, and that goes to their credibility. It's for us to assess. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, commenting is one thing. Giving evidence about -- giving evidence that may sustain comments by others is one thing, but commenting, being allowed simply to comment is another. Typically, witnesses aren't allowed simply to comment on the alleged credibility or veracity of witnesses. They have to give evidence. It's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what the witness is doing is giving evidence on the evidence that was given by Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If a witness is accused -- sorry, if a witness here is accused by another witness of saying something which the witness here thinks is a lie, why can't he say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He can say it's untrue. He can say it's untrue, of course he can. And he can also give factual reasons if factual reasons exist for supporting that, but we're getting very expansive answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think the comments you've made have merit in relation to the answer we've just been listening to, but speaking for myself, I think that the evidence this morning to a large extent has been very focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, to put aside the question of whether you said this to Dulovic or not, it says here that you said that in 1991 and 1992 the two of us cooperated closely and that I was supplying you with weapons, food, and so on and so forth. Do you remember having said this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I did say that more than once, speaking to different media, but this was part of the propaganda war in which your party was declaring me to be a criminal, a psychopath, an alcoholic, and so on and so forth, but this does not correspond to the facts. One has to bear in mind the characteristics of Serbian political life. For example, the previous regime said that I had participated in the murder of Djindjic. Later on, the Prime Minister said that they didn't mean it seriously. Then the government accused me of stealing 36 million Deutschmarks. We have to see all this in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think you answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over what period of time do you think we cannot rely on your public statements as accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every public statement has to be seen in the historical context in which it was made. As to whether they were false or true, in theory there is a very important standpoint. A lie is not something that is said in public and does not correspond to the facts if everybody knows it's not true. For example, the public was amused by the way I was accusing you of things that you hadn't done and how you're upset about this. However, here I'm testifying under oath about the facts. Our first conversation was in May 1991 and the first time we met was in April 1992. These are the only facts, and these can be proved. As for the rest, this is just Serbian political folklore. And I am not the only example of this. All the other participants in political life are as well. The Democratic Party would forge a document with a signature of mine. They would photocopy my signature from another document, and they would insert another text. You know, in Serbian political life a lot of things happened, and all this has to be borne in mind when judging public statements made by in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It also has to be borne in mind when judging statements made here, that people in other contexts quite deliberately lie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I am now speaking in public under oath and that's the difference. There's a difference between what one says when testifying before a court and what one can say in the heated political atmosphere when one is exchanging blows with one's opponents. And of course it's for you to evaluate the credibility of my testimony. I will not go into that. And the credibility of all the other testimonies here. I am fully aware of the circumstances of my testimony here and its historical import. History will study what I said here, not what I may have said in a heated debate, a heated political atmosphere where one day I'm opposed to someone and the next day we can cooperate again. However, I am fully conscious of the historical importance of my testimony here, whatever the outcome may be in terms of the Court's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dulovic, on page 11847, says that he knows for sure on the basis of his own investigations that members of Seselj's party volunteered to the local committees of the Serb Radical Party that made up lists, sent them to the Ministry of the Interior in order to be checked, and then the Ministry of the Interior sent lists further on or, rather, back to the local committees that then called the volunteers who had been approved. Now, my question is the following: Dulovic himself says that your volunteers signed up voluntarily. Did you send their names to the police for checks and did the police then give you approval as to who you would call to your local committees?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At first we had some volunteers who had not done their military service, their regular military service. When we understood that problem, when it was pointed out to us - I cannot remember all the details now - then we insisted that only those who had completed their regular military service could volunteer, those who had had some kind of military training before that, because it did happen that sometimes people applied without any military training beforehand and then they would get killed because of this total lack of military experience. So these checks simply never were carried out. Our municipal committees had the task of making sure that the persons concerned were not drug addicts. Drug addicts were definitely banned, then alcoholics, too, and notorious criminals. We avoided those three categories; drug addicts, alcoholics, and notorious criminals. Once the lists were made, then these volunteers were called to Belgrade, to the headquarters of the party, and from the headquarters of the party they were sent on buses to the barracks in Bubanj Potok and that is where they were put under the command of the relevant military authorities, and then the command sent them on to where they thought they would be used best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Help me to understand this. What you're saying is among your membership were drug addicts, alcoholics, and notorious criminals, but while they could be members of the party they couldn't serve --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- as volunteers. Well, could you explain how I've misunderstood that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You know, there is free membership in the Serb Radical Party. Anybody can become a member. Whoever wishes to do so, whoever is 18 years of age can do so. There are no bans, and also no checks are carried out previously to see what kind of a person the member is. It's a free party. Anybody can join. However, when personnel policies are pursued, then the criteria become more strict. In this case, it was made sure that among the volunteers there should be no drug addicts, alcoholics, or notorious criminals. It could happen that on a particular day a person could join the Serb Radical Party and say, "I wish to sign up as one of your volunteers." There were such cases. Then also some people who got in contact with our volunteers at the front line would join the Serb Radical Party there. I already mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I have the impression that it's very difficult for the transcript to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. You talked about "our municipal committees." Are these party committees or are these committees of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no committees of the Ministry of the Interior. These are committees of the Serb Radical Party that exist in all municipalities and also at lower levels of local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you did not answer part of my question that has to do with the Ministry of the Interior. Did you send information about your volunteers to the Ministry of the Interior so that they could assess who can be a volunteer and who cannot?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. And you can never find a document to that effect that we sent them such lists. It is absolutely impossible for such a document to exist. I think that you have received a very direct answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause. Could Mr. Milosevic stop before putting a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again the interpreters are asking for a pause between question and answer. It is particularly relevant, Mr. Seselj. You speak immediately. In fact, you speak before Mr. Milosevic has completed his question. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I was just consulting with my colleagues since they have more knowledge of these technical matters than I do. You have to observe the pause since you're listening in your own language, because if you are listening in the other language, then you can hear the interpretation, wait until it's finished, wait until the interpretation of the question is finished and then you start to speak. But since you're listening on a Serbian channel, then you must observe the pause. That's the only way. Otherwise, the interpreters will be asking me every five minutes to tell you to observe the pause. Mr. Milosevic is a veteran at this so he does a little better, but he was delinquent a short time ago. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 11848, when I said that the Serb Radical Party had never had any paramilitary formations, the witness answered that that was not true. I quoted you then, namely that you never had any paramilitary formations. He said that that was not correct. A few pages later on the transcript, in order to prove that there were such paramilitary formations, he mentions Seselj's unit the Yellow Wasps led by Major Dusan or Vojin Vuckovic. We already talked about that. So I claim that you did not have paramilitary formations. He says that is not correct, and then he refers to the Yellow Wasps. Is it necessary to give an additional explanation or do you believe that you have explained this fully? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Yellow Wasps, we had nothing to do with them. When members of the paramilitary formation called the Yellow Wasps were arrested and put in prison in Bijeljina, the Serb Radical Party issued an official statement, press release, supporting the arrest. That is an undeniable fact. Vojin Vuckovic, nicknamed Zuca, himself in his statement which was submitted to me as part of the exculpatory material testifies that at that time he had nothing to do with the Serb Radical Party. At the beginning of the war he was a member. In Western Slavonia he was a volunteer, but then, as he says, he left the party because we had cooperated with the regime. Actually, he was thrown out because of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I hope we have clarified that. Dulovic, on page 11874, says that when he was in Zvornik there was a clash between the Territorial Defence and a strong military -- paramilitary formation, and the man who led this paramilitary formation said that he was one of Seselj's men, and it was the same Cele that you mentioned a short while ago. He talks about a paramilitary formation headed by this man that was in a conflict with the Territorial Defence. So this was an inter-Serb conflict. He's not talking about a conflict with any other ethnic group here. He says that there was a paramilitary formation there headed by that person.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically claim that Miroslav Vukovic Cele was a volunteer in Zvornik within the JNA and that he had come to Zvornik as such. Now, whether he personally clashed there with some local Serbs or not is something that I don't know about. This is the first time I hear of this. And I cannot go into that. However, he left Zvornik when the JNA units withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not at the head of your paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no paramilitary formation of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C060 testified on the 21st of October, 2002. This is on transcript page 12004, saw in Vocin in October and November 1991 Seselj with Vukelic, Sasic, Bojcic, and others.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably saw me. Thousands of people saw me there. Veljko Vukelic at the time was Prime Minister of Western Slavonia. Ilija Sasic was minister of foreign affairs. He was the person who I came with by helicopter to Western Slavonia. We took a helicopter to Banja Luka and then from Banja Luka we went to Western Slavonia by car. Those are the facts. Thousands of people saw me there; Serbs, Croats, all of those who were there. I visited many places, I talked to many people, shook hands with many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn then of any crimes or any incidents that had occurred in that territory? I wish to remind you that in several of these statements there is mention of some local population or local extremists. Different terms were used in these statements that I've quoted to you. Have you heard anything about such things?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, at that time there weren't any such crimes. Some crimes had happened at the time of the fall of Western Slavonia. As for the type of crimes and who had committed them, the best explanation for that could be given by General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the then head of the then security service of the JNA who happened to be in Western Slavonia at the time of its fall. I was not there at the time of the fall of Western Slavonia. I was there almost a month before Western Slavonia fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Slobodan Lazarevic, who testified on the 30th of October, 2002, says that very early on, in the area of Knin, White Eagles appears, Seselj's volunteers, and Captain Dragan's volunteers. Did that coincide with what happened in Knin at the time? You were there for a while on several occasions, as you said yourself.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of the White Eagles being in Knin. There weren't any volunteers of the Serb Radical Party in Knin. The volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were at the Lika theatre of war, because the territory there was very big and with a very low density of the population. In Knin, there were enough local Serb soldiers. Captain Dragan had a training centre in Golubic, I think. That is near Knin, but I never visited that centre. I always kept my distance from Captain Dragan, considering him to be an ordinary criminal and a cheater.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Petar Kriste testified on the 27th of January, 2003. The page is 14925. He says that the rebellion in the Croatian territory was the result of activities of secret services and agents like Seselj and others who had come from Serbia for the most part. So what happened in Croatia was the result of activities of agents from Serbia, including you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an absolute fabrication. The Krajina Serbs themselves and collectively felt jeopardised by Tudjman's regime. That is why they stood up. I first came to Knin when the roadblocks had already been put in place for quite awhile. I came towards the end of August or beginning of September 1990. As far as I can remember the roadblocks had already been put up everywhere. No agents from Serbia could make the Krajina Serbs rebel, take up arms, had they not really been threatened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Aleksandar Vasiljevic, on the 6th of February, 2003, that is transcript page 15812, recalls that Seselj publicly, in a BBC TV programme called The Death Of Yugoslavia, so you publicly in that BBC TV programme, according to what Vasiljevic says, said that Jovica Stanisic had hired you to get some volunteers and that you took weapons from the JNA in order to arm them.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is a lie that I said that I was hired by Jovica Stanisic. I never could have said anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It would have been insulting.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. But that I pulled all stops when attacking Jovica Stanisic and made statements that I was sure would upset him the most is correct. At one point in time, when I heard that Jovica Stanisic was ill, I had pangs of a guilty conscience even. I was sort of wondering whether these attacks of mine had contributed to the psychosomatic basis of his illness. However, I did not feel that for a long period of time. I attacked Jovica Stanisic as head of the secret police using all conceivable means, because he started a political conflict with the Serb Radical Party. He started recruiting members of my party. We expelled Ljubisa Petkovic, vice-president of our party, because he was suspected of being recruited by the secret service. Also, there is video footage of seven of our MPs in the federal parliament who were given money to betray the party in order to tip the balance of power in the parliament. This was done by Jovica Stanisic. And on the other hand this was recorded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say that you used all conceivable means, did that include making inaccurate statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bombastic statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the two are quite different in my vocabulary. Perhaps not in yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to a particular fact, Mr. Bonomy. A prosecutor is sitting here, the one who is in charge of the proceedings against me. In her official motion to the Trial Chamber, she called me a scandalmonger, and I'm proud of that title. There is no greater scandalmonger in Serbian political life than me over the past 15 years. When I needed this kind of scandal out of political interests, I was the one who could do that the most skilfully. I am so proud of that title of scandalmonger that this lady sitting there bestowed upon me. I'm prouder than -- of that than of my doctorate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. There you have it. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it possible, Mr. Seselj, that you had said to the BBC people that you had been engaged by Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not impossible. I used that programme, too, to attack Jovica Stanisic, and here is why: In the preceding period, all the Western media and Western politicians were attacking Mr. Milosevic as the Balkans butcher, and they used many other terms. After the support given to Vance-Owen's Peace Plan all the way up to the Dayton Accords, Western politicians started praising Mr. Milosevic. After the Dayton Accords, the Americans publicly stated that he was the main guarantor of peace in the Balkans. And in the same period, I started to pull out those accusations against Mr. Milosevic and his associates that had been previously used by the West. So in that period, I didn't agree with him and I started repeating the same accusations that were presented by the West at the time when they were calling him the Balkans butcher and termed him uncooperative. When he became cooperative with them, then I started seeking quarrel with him, seeking scandal, and creating comedy sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you then specifically why you would say that Stanisic had hired you to get some volunteers and that you took weapons from the JNA in order to arm them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to provoke Stanisic to do something rash against me and the Serb Radical Party. I wanted to provoke him. I wanted that from the depth of my heart, and I was using every term and accusation that I could think of short of cursing his mother. He was chief of the secret police, a very powerful man, and he was working systematically to destroy the Serbian Radical Party. I don't have to tell you about the arsenal that is at the disposal of the secret police, how they use fabrications, lies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me point out to you one of the sessions of Aleksandar Vasiljevic on the 12th of February, six days into his testimony, on page 15934, when he says very decidedly: "Miodrag Lancuzanin was a commander of the Leva Supoderica unit that took part in the liquidations in Ovcara. This unit was called Seselj's unit. Practically, those were his radicals." So everything is lumped together. Leva Supoderica, Ovcara, the detachments, so you can conclude that this detachment of Seselj's perpetrated the execution in Ovcara. Tell me, what is the truth about this Leva Supoderica unit, and what is the truth about Miodrag Lancuzanin, its commander, and whether there is any link between the detachment and Lancuzanin with the execution in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an obvious example of false testimony by Aleksandar Vasiljevic. This Miodrag Lancuzanin - I'm not sure about his first name, maybe it's Milan - he was otherwise known as Kameni. He was the commander of the Leva Supoderica unit. Originally it was the defence detachment of Vukovar and he was a native of Vukovar and captain first class in reserve. When the Guards Brigade came to the area of Vukovar, then that detachment Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was resubordinated to the commander of the 1st Guards Brigade, and that commander decided that the volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party should be admitted into the detachment and become part of the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please stop for a moment. Let us clarify this very, very carefully. So there was a detachment of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar and its commander was a reserve officer, Lancuzanin.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your volunteers were included into that detachment as they would be included in any other JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not a complete definition. It was only when that detachment became part of the 1st Guards Brigade was the order issued that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party be admitted into that detachment. Before that, there were no volunteers of ours in that detachment and Kameni was not a member of our party. Kameni joined our party during the war when our volunteers started arriving to place themselves under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly now? Your volunteers came to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When this existing detachment, the authenticate Vukovar Territorial Defence detachment, became part of this JNA unit, the 1st Guards Brigade, then your volunteers were included in that unit as they were included in various other units?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that is clear enough. Now, tell me, this detachment and this particular person, this captain first class as you say, Lancuzanin, do they have anything to do with the events in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I heard about the crime in Ovcara, which was several months after the fact, I called Kameni to come to Belgrade, and I asked him to tell me whether he had participated in that. He swore on all that he could swear on that he had nothing to do with that crime, and I was persuaded he was telling the truth. When I came here, as part of the exculpatory material delivered to me by the OTP, and I mentioned this a moment ago, a profanity is used, and I didn't hear from Mr. Robinson whether he would allow me to quote it. That's something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If Mr. Milosevic feels it is important to his case, then you may use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's necessary. The point is, I suppose, the fact that you tried to explain a moment ago, namely that he was called all sorts of names because he wasn't with them at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Kameni got a whiff of something suspicious being in the offing, he got into his car and left. He didn't want to be part of it at any cost. After it happened, the people who took part in the execution called Kameni all sorts of names because he didn't participate. And documents testifying to this were delivered to me by the OTP. I hadn't known about them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That clarifies it sufficiently. Did anyone from that detachment, as far as you know, take part in the crime at Ovcara or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, nobody from that detachment took part. That's what Kameni told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any other member of the Serb Radical Party from that area, even if they were a native of that area, take part?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, one of the accused Stanko Vujanovic joined the Serbian Radical Party later, subsequently. Only in 1993. It was Rade Leskovac who introduced him as a member, then president of the Serbian Radical Party for the Republic of Serbian Krajina. He nominated him at the first party elections, majority elections, and Stanko Vujanovic became one of the majority MPs. I don't know whether he participated in the executions or not. We have to hear about that from the judgement of the Special Court for War Crimes in Belgrade. That judgement is pending and expected soon. But at the time of the liberation of Vukovar, he was not a member of the Serbian Radical Party. He became one only in 1993. That is an indisputable fact. Generally speaking, he's a native of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope this is not a major digression, but how do you explain that nobody knew about that event, even you who had a large number of volunteers on the ground? How come that nobody knew about it for several months after the fact?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's something you have to ask of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, because he was in Western Slavonia at the time. He was in the area of Vukovar, and when the execution happened, from what I know, the commander from the Guards Brigade, then Colonel, now General, Mrksic was not in Vukovar at all from what I know. General Vasiljevic was, and he should be asked why he hadn't filed criminal charges or a criminal report as soon as he found out, even if he didn't participate in organising that crime. And why he stole 1 million Deutschmarks from the Vukovar party. He never -- he never submitted that money through proper channels to the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was another witness here, Dragan Vasiljkovic, better known as Captain Dragan, on the 19th February, 2003. Page 6 -- or 16487. It says that Seselj had sent a bus carrying with self-styled Chetniks -- carrying self-styled Chetniks, people who called themselves Chetniks. Captain Dragan stopped the bus because he considered that to be his own responsibility, whereas the bus was headed for Korenica. He sent 15 per cent of the people from the bus back to Belgrade and recruited the rest into his own unit. Do you remember such an event, such a problem with Dragan Vasiljkovic and those Chetniks that were sent to Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Vasiljkovic is a false captain who had been brought there by somebody to run that centre in Golubic. I don't see how Korenica could possibly be his zone of responsibility. He may have been there. It's just that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party didn't go there by bus. They went there by plane. And they would land in JNA planes to the Udbina air field. It's possible that some volunteers were interviewed by him, and he may have rejected some of them. I don't know about that. But he never had any problem with me on that score. The first time he had a problem with me was in November 1991, when he came to Knin again, because he had come once before and was turned away by Martic. He was in their way, and the officers complained that he didn't know his job and he was trying to teach them. It was the media who spread this story about him as an able officer. So when he came to Knin to organise that putsch, I met him at the first front line, forward defence line in Benkovac, and that meeting was recorded on camera. I think it was precisely Miroslav Mlinar, whom I mentioned before as the man who had been badly beaten by Croats so that he barely survived before the conflict broke out. So he was the man who recorded my public duel with Dragan Vasiljkovic. I attacked him publicly, saying that he was a criminal. And later when he established that fund to assist the war veterans and their families and the families of those who had fallen in the war, I said that -- and they -- and I said that he stole money from that fund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I really want to see that -- how the interpreters translated that particular bit when you said that he was trying -- that he was trying to dispense wisdom to the officers. They simply said tried to teach them their job.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know English, but I suggest that the records be reviewed after this trial and maybe the interpreters will find better solutions when they have more time after this trial is over. They might find better solutions than what they did on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my next question -- on page 16490, Dragan Vasiljkovic says that he doesn't accept that any unit could act independently, and that goes for Seselj's units too.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that I agree with that witness. Nobody there could act independently. Everybody was part of the JNA in that western part of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 16513, the witness says Vojislav Seselj, waving a gun, threatened the students of the law school of the university in Belgrade. "The students came to see me, asking for protection, carrying weapons themselves." The witness was worried. He disarmed the children, and he told them to go to the Ministry of the Interior and complain, and if they are not given any protection, he would protect them themselves. He said he had asked Radmilo Bogdanovic to strip Seselj of immunity because of this incident with the students. Which part, if any, of this is true? Was there an incident at the law school? Was it in the street?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, this is false testimony by Dragan Vasiljkovic. There were no students. They were rabble, rabble who attacked me as I was coming out of the building of the Assembly as an MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was rabble, not students of the law school?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been law students among the rabble. They threw stones at me and bottles of water, and when my life was really threatened, when the rabble had come really close, I took the gun out of my pocket, I pointed it in the air and threatened them, and the rabble pulled back immediately. They balked. In that group, in that rabble there were criminals as well, like Vojislav Bozilovic and Snezana Rajcic, a student and assistant Dean of the law school, who were arrested several weeks later for the murder of a shop assistants -- shop assistant in the jewellery called Majdanpek near the Terazije square. That's the kind of students we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were later arrested, you say.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were convicted. I think this Bozilovic got 15 years' imprisonment for this robbery and murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C048, on the 28th of April, 2003, said that Seselj gathered and trained people in Bubanj Potok. Did you gather and train men in Bubanj Potok?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were being sent, I was never in Bubanj Potok. When I was serving my regular military service in Belgrade in 1980, on two occasions I was in Bubanj Potok. Once as a young soldier I was taken there to -- for target practice, and another time I as a squad leader took young soldiers there for target practice. That was in 1980. My collaborators in the party visited Bubanj Potok, perhaps, but I personally never did because there was no need. This was a technical job for volunteers to be taken from the party headquarters to Bubanj Potok. So why should I go there personally? I usually held speeches to these volunteers in front of the headquarters of the Serb Radical Party or somewhere else in the centre of Belgrade. I spoke to them of chivalry on the battlefield, that they should be courageous and that they should be disciplined, and that they should treat prisoners of war, civilians, and the wounded humanely, as true chivalrous knights do. That was the essence of the speeches I made, and many journalists attended these send-offs and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they can testify to all this. Why should I go to Bubanj Potok? I never went to the General Staff at the time either. Why should I? Other people from my party did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in these proceedings witness Renaud de la Brosse on several occasions mentioned you in connection with these charges being brought against me. On the 20th of May, 2003, on transcript page 20776, he said Seselj drew up a list for the elimination of some journalists from Germany which he read out on television. When he mentions this list, what is this about?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard any greater nonsense at this Hague Tribunal. I did make statements that I had SS-20 rockets at my disposal and that I would target the American military base Aviano in Italy. This caused panic in Italy. All the media wrote about it. And by this statement I delayed the bombing of Republika Srpska by at least six months. That's how effective this bombastic statement of mine was. But I never made such a statement about German journalists nor did I read out such a list on television. I did know some German journalists. I occasionally gave them interviews. For example, a certain Havlovic, a German who was a correspondent of a German television station. I knew Renata Flot, who was a correspondent of Spiegel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you might have missed your calling. You should be a PR consultant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I leave this prison in some 40 to 50 years, if you offer me such a job I will be happy to accept, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, 5th Avenue in New York might be interested. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the same witness, Renaud de la Brosse, on transcript page 2805 of the same day said, "Seselj influenced public opinion by speaking of Croatian crimes from World War II." In what context did you speak about Croatian crimes from World War II, and was your intention in mentioning these crimes to influence public opinion in a negative way?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these crimes were truly horrendous, and proportionally greater than Hitler's crimes, because the Croats in World War II committed more crimes and more horrendous crimes than the Germans did when viewed in proportion. This is a historical fact. Secondly, the Serb public was well-informed about these crimes. Thirdly, I did often mention these crimes and the fact that most of the perpetrators had remained unpunished because, with the help of the Vatican, they managed to flee to South America. And the Croatian Ustasha leader Pavelic managed to reach South America with the help of the Vatican. This remains deep in the memory of the Serb people who are afraid that such crimes might be repeated. As a politician, I was constantly trying to influence public opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't question the fact that public statements made by politicians have the purpose of influencing public opinion. My question was did you do this with the intention of causing negative consequences?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wanted to cause positive consequences, for the Serb people not to allow such terrible crimes to be perpetrated against them again, to be exposed to genocide again. And Tudjman was openly advocating this, announcing this in his speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2835, this same witness says, "Seselj publicly made threats against the Muslims." Did you in public in your various political speeches threaten the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. I was constantly trying to win over the Muslims and to avoid a conflict in Bosnia. You can look at the contents of my speech at the large rally in Banja Luka sometime in November 1991, which I held on my return from Western Slavonia. The large Boric Hall [phoen] was full to overflowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters have asked me to bring to your attention the fact that when you read from the transcript which you are quoting to the witness, you are reading much too fast for them. You have been reading the transcript evidence of witness -- of Prosecution witnesses, but you tend to read too fast for them to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, there was a witness here, C047. He testified on the 3rd of June, 2003, and the pages of the transcript are 21584 to 588. He states that he met Seselj in 1990 in Mali Stapar, a restaurant owned by Aleksandar Nikolic. There, Seselj said there would be war and that he was advocating a monarchy and that an army should be organised to fight and topple communism in Yugoslavia and Serbia. The Croats were exerting pressure on the Serbs in Croatia, and his army was already organising in Western Backa, headed by Jovo Ostojic. Jovo Ostojic organised and trained men for the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are nebulous statements. This has nothing to do with reality. First of all, I never advocated a monarchy. I have always been a republican. I think only an idiot in the Serbia of today could advocate a monarchy and that no one in Serbia is in favour of a monarchy. That's one thing. Secondly, I never wanted to topple the communist regime using weapons. And the army, I always advocated the toppling of the communist regime by peaceful means. In 1990, Jovo Ostojic could not have been a member of the Serb Radical Party because it didn't exist at the time. All that existed was the Serb Renewal Movement or the Serb Chetnik Movement. I don't recall any meeting in that cafe. It's not impossible that I happened to be in Stapar, but this does not correspond to the truth. It's impossible that I could have said something like this. Jovo Ostojic joined the Serb Radical Party only in 1992. As far as I know, before that he had been a member of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 21594, this same witness C047 says that the Serb Chetnik Movement was organising to provide assistance to Slavonia, Baranja, and Krajina. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted to provide assistance. This was in 1990. I have already told you that I travelled to Knin, that Milan Babic was seeking volunteers, that I tried to gather volunteers, that your police arrested me for that reason, that I was sentenced to 15 days in prison for a misdemeanour. On two occasions in that year I was sentenced to 20 and 25 days in prison respectively because of demonstrations in front of the federal Assembly in support of the Krajina Serbs. In the year 1990, I took up my candidacy for president of the republic from prison. I appeared on TV only once and gained a hundred thousand votes, but in that year there was no possibility of providing concrete assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. This same witness - and these are pages 21601 and 602 - says: "Seselj held a rally in Subotica in 1990 at which he said -" that is at a rally in Subotica in 1990 - "that he would use a rusty fork to gouge out the eyes of non-Serbs, Croats and Hungarians in Subotica who were not loyal to the local authorities." He said that the Croats should be expelled to Croatia and that the Serbs should be returned to their homes. He said the same about the Hungarians. He spoke of the borders of a Greater Serbia from Karlovac to Karlobag and Virovitica. So in 1990 you are gouging out eyes with a rusty spoon at a rally in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an absolute lie. There was no rally in Subotica in that year. What the Serb Radical Party did was in November 1991, it held its first rally in Subotica then, and that meeting was attended by about 5.000 people. Those 5.000 people can testify that I never said anything like that. Absolutely not. The Prosecution is relying on witness Vesna Kljaic, who says that just before that rally I danced a round dance, and I have never danced that dance in my life. I'm not a musical man. I have no sense of rhythm and I never danced that dance. So we are facing nonsense. In June 1991, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I think you have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- I know you're coming to 1991, but just for the record, the very witness clarified later the year in which you held the rally in Subotica is in 1991, not 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I am denying that I said anything like that at the rally. I want to let you know that this witness of yours is testifying falsely based on a statement I made in a show called Minimaks Ilic, a comedy show hosted by Milovan Ilic Minimaks, a famous Serb comedian, and I took part in June 1991. When asked directly by him in a facetious tone, "Are you Chetniks still cutting throats?" I responded, "Oh, yes. Only we've changed our methods of slaughter. We no longer use knives, we use rusty shoehorns so that one cannot tell whether the victim was killed by slaughter or died of tetanus." This was black humour. It may not be everybody's cup of tea. I like it. But this was never said at a rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's now for Mr. Milosevic to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This comedy show is well known in Serbia, Mr. Seselj, and you have explained again now what this was about. So not only did you not hold a rally, but you never said anything like that at any rally, is that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Minimaks died a few months ago, and to pay homage to him the Politika TV station in Belgrade broadcast that show again and the Serb public was reminded of its contents. This was two or three months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This Witness 047 says that in Subotica he saw Seselj, Ostojic, and Kertes. Weapons were being distributed; rifles, automatic rifles, and so on. This was done by Seselj, Ostojic, and JNA officers. This is on page 21607 and 608.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a lie. Jovo Ostojic might have attended a meeting in Subotica. I never met Kertes in Subotica, and there was never any distribution of weapons in Subotica. This witness is lying absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same witness, C047, on the same day - the transcript is 21641 - says Seselj held a rally in Subotica and Novi Zednik in May 1992 at which he gave the example of Hrtkovci as to what should be done and how the Croats and the Hungarians were to be forced to leave of their own accord. If they failed to do so, other violent measures should be used.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an absolute fabrication. I never mentioned Hungarians in any negative context whatsoever. In May 1992, I did have a rally in Hrtkovci on the 6th of May, and at that rally, which was part of the election campaign for the forthcoming federal elections, I advocated the so-called retortion principle. As Tudjman's regime had expelled several hundreds of thousands of Serbs from Croatia, at this election rally I publicly advocated that, according to the principle of reciprocity, Serbia should return this because of the feeling of desperation because of these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hundreds of thousands of expelled Serbs, I advocated an exchange of property. I asked that the expelled Serbs look for Croats with whom they could exchange property in order to mitigate this refugee crisis. At this rally, I am alleged to have read out a list of Croats to be expelled. That's a lie. I didn't read out any lists. An activist of the Serb Radical Party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll stop if you're not interested in hearing any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You advocated retortion at an election rally.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever take any practical measures to carry out this in practice?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No practical measures. We just promised that if we came to power, but we didn't come to power. What we said then was said out of anger and out of despair at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same witness, C047, said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milosevic. In previous answer you said at the end of that part: "At this rally I'm alleged to have read out a list of Croats to be expelled. That's a lie. I didn't read out any list." Then you said "An activist of the Serb Radical Party --" and you stopped. What were you trying to say at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I wasn't the one who stopped. Mr. Robinson interrupted me. But see how overwhelming my respect is that I always abide by what he says. I wish to answer that question, though. An activist of the Serb Radical Party read out the names of Croats from Hrtkovci who had gone to Croatia and joined the ZNG of Franjo Tudjman in order to wage war against the Serbs there. We have video footage of that rally. And in this same book that I showed a short while ago, The Criminal Pope John Paul II; The Devil's Apprentice, I gave a recording of that rally. We also have video footage of that. I am preparing for my own trial to use that. That is to say, to show it in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can spare us the exaggeration in language, Mr. Seselj. I don't want any prolongation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want -- I wish you could tell me what was so bombastic so that I would avoid doing it in the future, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The reference to the Pope. That's what I characterise as a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a title of my book. What can I do about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't wish to prolong this. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this witness, on transcript page 21720, talked about the promotion of officers on the 9th of December, 1991, signed by Katic, commander of the volunteers, sent by Seselj for a particular part of Vukovar. What kind of promotion of officers is this signed by your commander of volunteers? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Slobodan Katic, as far as I can remember, at a given point in time was the deputy of Milan Lancuzanin Kameni in the Leva Supoderica Detachment. I know him very well. He's a member of the Serb Radical Party and a volunteer. Now, formally there couldn't have been any promotion. It is possible that somewhere someone promoted an officer of his own free will as an arbitrary act, but this was not relevant to the military command organs or was it part of one's service book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 21741, this same witness, C047, says Seselj was in opposition but he secretly collaborated with the authorities. Tell us now, how was it that you secretly collaborated with the authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite impossible. Whenever I cooperated with the authorities, I did that openly and publicly. When we supported the minority government in 1993, we did it publicly and openly. And we explained to people why we did not want to join that government. Later, when we went into the coalition, we did that openly. When we were in a conflict, that was open too. In periods of conflicts, there were no contacts between us; and when we cooperated, then there were contacts. I already mentioned those numerous meetings and talks we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, what the witness claims, that you secretly collaborated with the authorities while you were in opposition, is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness says on page 21965 that, "Seselj got a great amount of money when Djuic appointed him vojvoda to fight against communism." Did you really get a very large amount of money from Djuic or anybody when Djuic appointed you vojvoda to fight against communism?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a fabrication. I earned some money while selling my books when visiting the Serb emigration, and also I lectured in these different Serb organisations that were registered as humanitarian organisations according to the laws there. I never got any amount of money from Djuic. Once he did send some money, in May 1991, that is to say $500. He sent them through a Serb Orthodox priest from America. That money was given out to some volunteers who took part in the fighting in Borovo Selo and who were poor otherwise. I now remember that Miladin Todosijevic got a certain amount. Some was received by Oliver Denis Baret and a few others, but that was the only financial contribution of Momcilo Djuic from the moment when our party came into existence all the way up to his death. We never received any other money from him. When American congressman Jim Moody was in Belgrade and when he personally requested a special meeting with me, trying to persuade me to have a showdown with your government, and I retorted in very strong words by attacking the ambassador in Belgrade, Zimmerman, because of his anti-Serb policy. He was very angry about this and then Djuic stopped all contact with me. After that, we had only a few contacts but they were really forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The transcript, like the translation, reads 500 dollars. It may be that that was an error. I think it may be 5.000. It's worth checking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said 5.000, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what a priest brought in May 1991. I think that in the Serb Radical Party we have the name of that priest recorded. I cannot remember right now. He is either from Chicago or Milwaukee, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this witness says that he thinks that Seselj wrote - and the transcript page is 21995 - part of the programme of the Serb Radical Party in 1991 where it is said that 360.000 Albanians have to be expelled straight away.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple to find that programme and to see what it says. That programme was published in our newspaper, in the newspaper called Velika Srbija, Greater Serbia, it was published in my books, and it says that Albanian emigres should be expelled, those who do not have our citizenship. And the estimate was that from World War II onwards there were 360.000 of them who illegally entered from Albania and engaged in separatist activity. So this pertains to Albanian emigres only, people who did not have our citizenship. The programme of the Serb Radical Party is something that we worked on collectively, and it is a matter of course that I played the main role in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not the point here, whether you wrote the programme of your party.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's only natural. It's a bit tendentious, as if that witness knew exactly which part I wrote. I had the main say in all of this and I took part in the writing of the entire programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This same witness says, on transcript page 21997, that on the 2nd of February, 1994, Seselj and Babic had a joint press conference at which they stated that the two strongest parties in the Krajina have to cooperate in promoting a joint objective of the priority national interests of Republika Srpska and the Serb Krajina. Seselj stated then that these two territories should become part of a single state. That was the agreement between Babic and Seselj. After that, the Serb Radical Party became part of the Krajina government. So this is the 2nd of February, 1994, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement is partly true and partly untrue. What is incorrect is that after that we joined the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina. We remained an opposition political party. At the beginning of 1994, we went into a coalition with the party of Milan Babic. On that occasion, Milan Babic came to Belgrade. We made public our coalition in the Tanjug press centre in Belgrade. We had a press conference. We published the entire content of that press conference, and it can be found in my books. At that time, we presented the entire programme of our government, and my personal wish was that the Republic of Srpska and the Republic of Serb Krajina would unite in a single state which would be called Western Serbia. Milan Babic was not inclined to accept that idea at the time. As far as I can remember, that was not our joint position at the time, it was only my position. We Radicals at that time published a newspaper, Western Serbia, in Banja Luka. Our party in Republika Srpska published it. We thought that this was one of the desirable variants of protecting Serb national interests. However, soon after that Milan Babic betrayed our agreement on a coalition. He entered the government of Borislav Mikelic and from then on we became political foes. Bitter ones at that. We were far angrier with Milan Babic for having trampled upon our agreement than Borislav Mikelic, with whom we disagreed in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness, C047, says on transcript page 21604 that a Catholic church was attacked in Subotica. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that attack. For the most part there weren't any such attacks in Serbia. In a few cases this could have occurred as an individual incident, but the Serb Radical Party never had anything to do with any attacks on places of worship. We were never against the Catholic faith. We appreciate those who profess the Catholic faith just like we respect those who are Orthodox and those who are Muslim. We are against the Vatican because of its politics, not because of theology. After all, if you look at the difference between the Orthodox and the Catholics, you will see that these differences are insignificant. For us ordinary believers, these differences are insignificant. Our problem is the politics of the Vatican, not their religious principles. We have the highest respect for those of the Catholic faith, of the Islamic faith, for as long as they are honest and honourable persons and --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A witness testified here under the code name C017. So this is a different witness, and he mentioned you several times. Let us just go through a few things now. If these allegations are correct. He says on page 22016 of the transcript that he saw Seselj's men in Buna. Buna is a small town near Mostar. I imagine that is the one he's talking about. He testified on the 10th of June, 2003. Were your people there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they got to Buna at all. Volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were within the JNA at the Mostar front under the command of Momcilo Perisic in 1991. That was before the actual war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the time when the Croatian paramilitary formations had taken Western Herzegovina and confronted themselves with the JNA at the Neretva River. That is when volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were sent from Serbia within the JNA to the Mostar front line and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have answered that question. You have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This witness says that at the camp in Buna he saw the headquarters of the Serb Chetnik Movement, that is to say Seselj's men and the White Eagles belonging to Jovic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a total fabrication. First of all, there were no headquarters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is pointless in view of the answer you've already given, which is that you have idea whether they got to Buna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the other thing hasn't got anything to do with Buna. With your permission, I would like to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question that was put was, "The witness says that at the camp in Buna he saw the headquarters of the Chetnik Movement." It's very simple. It plainly has to do with Buna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He mentioned on page 22023 that a certain Svabo was commander of Seselj's men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible that there was a headquarters of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. The question was whether there was a certain Svabo who was a commander of Seselj's men, of your men. Is that correct? We're not talking about the headquarters now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I remember some part of this witness's testimony was done in private session. So could you attend to that matter, whether it is all right to mention those parts in public session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a volunteer with the nickname of Svabo. Whether he was engaged in the Mostar theatre of war I cannot tell you now, but I know a very prominent capable volunteer, a courageous one nicknamed Svabo, he lives in Zemun in Belgrade. I can't remember his real name right now. I can find out by tomorrow if that's important. I can call people from my party so they can tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not particularly important. I just wanted to establish whether he was a commander of some sort and whether there was headquarters of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no headquarters of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and I never heard about White Eagles appearing in that area, not in the Mostar theatre of war. As far as I know, there were no White Eagles there. There were only volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party distributed across the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that would suffice. This Witness C17 says on page 22030, "All Seselj's men had a 27-day training at the camp in Golubic, and they were also in Borovo Selo." This Golubic camp is in the area of Knin. He says: "All Seselj's Chetniks passed through this training course that lasted 27 days."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That camp was run by Captain Dragan. I do not rule out the possibility that certain volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were sent for training there. I don't believe all of them went there. It's impossible. But it's possible that certain individual commands of the JNA had sent some volunteers there for training. As for Borovo Selo, I explained that in detail on my first or second day here. That was in the end of April or early May 1991, before the JNA openly went into armed conflict with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up one thing. No matter where your volunteers went for training, that was always organised by the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could not apply for training as private citizens. If there was any training, that must have been advanced training compared to what they had learnt during their regular military service. If it concerned handling weapons or retraining for a different speciality, like somebody was a signalsman and supposed to serve as a -- as a gunner now, then they needed additional training. But I cannot tell you exactly because I had never visited that camp in Golubic and I don't know who was sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same witness says on pages 22036 and 044, he mentions some names and nicknames. Do nicknames Kiza and Vranjanac mean anything to you? Do these people belong to the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they can't mean anything to me because everybody called Zoran has a -- the nickname of Kiza. Even Zoran Djindjic was called Kiza. Vranjanac means somebody who was born in the town of Vranje, so it means nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not bother you with the assertions that we've heard here. This witness says during the main offensive of the Muslims in Trnovo in 1995, there was Slavko Aleksic of the Serbian Chetniks. Were there any Chetnik units in 1995 in the area of Sarajevo or was it the army of Republika Srpska? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Aleksic was the commander of one unit of the army of Republika Srpska at the Jewish cemetery in Sarajevo. That was the site of the most frequent and fiercest battles with Muslims. Everybody from that area knows it. Slavko Aleksic is not a volunteer from the Serbian Radical Party who had been sent from Serbia. He is a native of Herzegovina. He lived in Sarajevo, and that's how he joined the Serbian Radical Party. And as soon as the war started, he joined the Serbian army. He became very prominent as a fighting man, and I bestowed upon him the title of Chetnik duke for his merits. When Biljana Plavsic became a renegade and joined the Western forces, he sided with Biljana Plavsic and I cut off all relations with him. Otherwise, he was a very good fighting man and he was particularly prominent in the battles of Trnovo. He's very famous and very well respected in that area. When you mention his name in Trnovo, everybody will tell you he's courageous and deserves a lot of credit for military success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 22112, this same witness says: "Among Chetniks volunteers, there were many criminals from Sarajevo, more precisely from the Grbavica area." Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely untrue. There were no criminals among our volunteers. If a criminal did crop up, we would eliminate him immediately. We took great care and made sure that none were included in our ranks. All our volunteers were part of JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you clarify one thing more precisely, because we are dealing with the testimony of an expert witness for the other side. Reynaud Theunens an officer who testified on the 26th of January, 2004, at transcript pages 31478, and I would really like to have this cleaned up finally. He's talking about the links between the JNA and the Territorial Defence and the volunteers in Vukovar, which has been explained to some extent already, and he says that Leva Supoderica unit was involved and the commander of Seselj's unit is on the payroll. Was he confused here? Was Seselj's unit part of the JNA or was it a local Territorial Defence unit that became part of the JNA later?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would be only happy if all the units that took part in that war in 1991 were called Seselj's units, but we already established that that unit was part of the 1st Guards Brigade, and of course they were on the payroll of that brigade. There's no doubt about it. I believe the Office of the Prosecutor has in its possession the order whereby that unit was brought under the wing of the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same witness says on page 31482: "Seselj's men are considered as volunteers but in some publications they are referred to as paramilitaries." He's only explaining the references he finds in different documents. Your definition is volunteers within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he obviously comes across these references in documents. However, our political opponents insist on calling them paramilitary units, which is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what he says here. Some publications called them paramilitaries. But you've just explained there were no cases when volunteers formed paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 31488, he says: "Seselj and his men were within the command structure of the JNA, and they were subordinated to the lowest level."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he means by that, "subordinated to the lowest Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. level." Does he mean to discredit us or what? They were within the structure of the JNA, and they were never grouped in greater numbers than one company. I hope he was not meaning to offend us. I didn't have my own school to produce military officers. They were all patriots who wished to fight for their country, and in a moment of crisis we sent them to the JNA, and they were not grouped together in greater numbers than one company, not to disturb the structure of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
